doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Sessions and teaching in New Orleans
title: Raising his own children on the instrument
summary: His kids heard him and Alvin Batiste practice; he wanted them to have solid technique, and Kent, Marlon and Rachel played classical solos and attended Tanglewood and Eastman.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: Did the same thing go for your own children? Did they hear you practice?

They used to hear me practice but then they’d hear their uncle Alvin Batiste practice and it’s a funny thing about my kids. They never did — Kent can hear how to play any kind of way. But jazz is such a personal thing that the thing about jazz, there’s a whole lot of people want to play a certain way but they don’t have the motor skills to play a certain way. They don’t have the rhythmic thing in order to play a certain way. This is why I’ve seen people sit down and learn, I can listen to somebody play sometimes and tell they’ve got everything correct but they don’t have whatever — sometimes it’s going against the old system. Like today some of them kids, I was looking and they was on the wrong beat but they was playing it. And like I told the kids about crossing their legs, remember? See all of that is a part of the thing. And I’d rather get a kid who got all of that and we can deal with the other stuff. But you can deal with all that academic stuff and you won’t get that and that will be a stumbling block for the jazz thing.

I couldn’t agree with you more. I mean you can’t teach a kid — you know it’s funny the first day, I should tell the people who are watching this that you’ve been doing a Louis Armstrong camp. And the first day I came down to watch a little bit and you were talking about tough love. And you said Kent knows about tough love. And then today when you were talking about, some of you guys were playing with your legs crossed, you’d better stop doing that or you’re going to be limping on the way home. Right?
I mean this is serious business, right?

But you see another thing about my kids, I wanted them to get a good firm grasp of the instrument. So Kent played, I don’t know if he told you, Kent played a solo with the orchestra at eleven years old of Mozart. And Marlon, you know Marlon my younger son?

Marlon played the piccolo trumpet solo in “The Rite of Spring” up there in Tanglewood when he was about twelve years old under Leonard Bernstein. So they was going, and my daughter Rachel, she was going at camp, she went to Tanglewood and Eastman and all of them. I wanted them to get a good grasp of the instrument, a good, well not classical grasp but I mean a good grasp of the instrument, how to play the instrument. See that’s another thing with jazz. A lot of people want to play jazz and that’s why it’s so limited because they don’t have the technical facility to go on and do what they’re talking about doing. And some people have to spend so much time trying to do some things and they don’t have the technical ability, over and over and over, whereas if they’d done their technical ability then you could do that.
